source.title: Toy Models of Superposition in the dense regime

record.tranche_reason: Extends toy-model superposition experiments into a range of lower-sparsity, denser settings and reports learned solution geometries.
record.gate_note: The post reports learned polygon configurations and a dimension-allocation example, which bear on the claim. LLC trajectories and loss-versus-LLC comparisons are not extracted as rows because they do not measure the claim versions. Captions that only say a figure shows fractions of configurations, without stating a result, are also not rows.
record.test_reason: Trains 6→2 toy autoencoders over sparsities 0.426–1 under optimal-hexagon and random 4-gon initialization. It reports the learned polygon geometries, which bears directly on V1's sparsity-dependent geometry in a denser setting than the original.
record.authors_conclusion: Broadly correct. Add that the authors report lower-loss solutions tend to have higher LLC, that models cluster at discrete loss plateaus, and that random initialization yields dead neurons, which explain its higher average loss. The work is explicitly incomplete and exploratory.
record.recipe_differences: Toy autoencoders with sparse synthetic inputs and geometric solution analysis; this post sweeps into denser settings and compares optimal high-sparsity initialization with random 4-gon initialization. Exact recipe equivalence to the original source is not stated.
record.method_sensitivity: Solution geometry and losses vary with sparsity and initialization; the authors also note that a step size of 0.05 would make hexagons more common in a few checked random-initialization runs.

fits_no_version.finding: Lower-loss solutions tend to have higher LLC estimates. LLC rises until S=0.892 and then falls at early training.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Solution complexity (LLC) trades off against loss across toy-model superposition solutions.

record.problems: The authors say the project is incomplete. Most geometry findings are qualitative; counts and uncertainty estimates are not reported in the text. The post notes that LLC absolute values depend heavily on hyperparameters. Some conclusions are based on selected illustrated runs, and the two descriptions of the best-performing geometries at sparsity 0.426 differ.
record.rows_left_out: Figures 22-31 are described as showing fractions of polygon configurations over training, but the text gives no specific values or trends to extract. The LLC and loss progression figures are not rows because they do not directly measure the claim versions.

untested.parts: Pairwise feature overlap or near-orthogonality and interference are not measured. No formal phase diagram or transition point is given. Feature importance is not varied.
All features have equal importance; the importance-based allocation of dedicated versus shared dimensions is not tested.
No LLMs or SAEs are studied.

missing.what: Run 476 (random 4-gon, S=0.811): the lowest-loss, highest-LLC run is still a sticky 4-gon.
Run 78 (S=0.426): 3 dimensions collapsed to near-zero weights with large negative biases, i.e. dead neurons.
Methodological caveats: input distribution forces at least one active binary entry, and the global minimum is noted to differ from the prior paper's classified solution.
Dendrogram clustering finds that models cluster mainly by number of negative biases.

record.verdict_notes: An informal LessWrong post; most results are qualitative, and the k-gon fraction plots have no described values. The record's 0.426 descriptions conflict (5-gons versus hexagon or triangle). Hexagon findability under random initialization depended on step size, per the authors' few checks.

versions.untested_parts: The post does not directly measure pairwise feature overlap, near-orthogonality, interference, or a formal sparsity-dependent transition.
It does not vary feature importance or establish that important features get dedicated dimensions while less important ones share.
No alternative cause of polysemanticity is tested.
No LLM activations or dictionary features are studied.
The post describes encoder-weight polygons, but does not test whether the represented features are one-dimensional rather than multidimensional.

rows.subject: autoencoders (triangle solution)
rows.operation_detail: Described how the triangle solution allocates its hidden dimensions.
rows.value: One hidden dimension is used to encode 1 output dimension, while the other encodes the remaining 5; the authors describe this as wasting an entire embedding dimension.
rows.locator: Results, discussion of lowest-loss solutions in the dense regime
rows.note: The authors suggest these models may get stuck in this solution when a bias starts relatively large. This is an example of unequal allocation under a bottleneck, not a test of feature importance.
rows.check: All six features have equal importance, so a 1-vs-5 split of hidden dimensions cannot test V2's importance-based allocation. The authors attribute it to a large initial bias (getting stuck), not to capacity competition. Remove the V2 link.

relationships.condition: Optimal or lowest-loss solutions, 6→2 autoencoders, binary inputs
relationships.reason: Hexagons (6 features in 2 dimensions) are optimal at S 0.964–1. The polygons shrink toward pentagons, 4-gons and 3-gons as density rises, a sparsity-dependent regular geometry (r1, r3, r5, r6, r13, r16, r17, r19).
relationships.display_finding: Hexagons holding 6 features in 2 dimensions were optimal at S 0.964–1, and the optimal polygons shrank to pentagons, 4-gons and 3-gons as density rose.

source_check.reason: r1, r3, r5, r6, r16, r17 and r19 report hexagonal and other polygonal representations whose geometry changes with sparsity. The S=0.426 descriptions are inconsistent, so they do not establish a monotonic shrinkage across the entire sweep.

relationships.reason: Random initialization rarely finds the optimal hexagon. Dead neurons and collapsed dimensions raise loss, and the same sparsity yields several geometries and irregular polygons. The geometry found depends on initialization and optimization (r2, r4, r11, r12, r15, r20, r21, r22).
relationships.display_finding: Random initialization rarely found the optimal hexagon, and dead neurons and collapsed dimensions raised loss. The same sparsity gave several geometries and irregular polygons, so the geometry depended on initialization and optimization.

source_check.label: limits_scope
source_check.reason: r2 reports infrequent recovery of optimal hexagons; r11, r12, r15 and r20–r22 report dead features, irregular geometry or trapping in suboptimal configurations. These support an optimization qualification; coexistence of polygon types alone does not.

relationships.reason: Even at S=0.426 the best solutions still superpose 5–6 features (5-gons, or a hexagon with positive biases). The transition differs from a simple drop to dedicated dimensions, though the input distribution differs from the original (r7, r8, r14).
relationships.display_finding: The best solutions still superposed 5–6 features (pentagons, or a hexagon with positive biases) instead of switching to dedicated dimensions. The input distribution differed from the original's, however.

relation.reason: Its own training results measure sparsity-dependent superposition geometries and initialization dependence, directly bearing on V1.

tranche.reason: The study extends toy-model geometry measurements to denser, conditioned binary inputs and compares two initialization schemes.

source_check.notes: The study is exploratory: reported lowest-loss solutions are empirical findings, not certified global optima, and dead neurons are proposed as an explanation for higher loss. The source contains inconsistent dense-regime geometry descriptions and prints the binary-one probability as S-1; its footnote gives 1-S for the earlier generator.

statements.correction: S=0.426: one results bullet identifies positive-bias pentagons as lowest-loss solutions; the later lowest-loss discussion describes positive-bias hexagons and a triangle configuration slightly above MSE 0.15; Figure 9 retains a hexagon; Figure 10 reports a 4-gon near loss 0.25. Inputs always contain at least one active entry.
statements.problem: The surviving superposition and inconsistent geometry descriptions are reported, but interpreting them as a scope limitation assumes a dedicated-dimension transition that V1 does not specify.
